lha-7.t: How many Americans know that after two U.S. Navy warships were blown open by sea mines in the Persian Gulf in 1991, five hundred and eleven Japanese sailors sa…
lha-7.tx:
How many Americans know that after two U.S. Navy warships were blown open by sea mines in the Persian Gulf in 1991, five hundred and eleven Japanese sailors sailed wooden boats straight into the deadliest minefield on earth to clear the way for the American fleet?

In February 1991, Iraqi mines tore holes in the amphibious assault ship USS Tripoli and the guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton. Over one thousand mines still choked the waters off Kuwait.

Western television commentators mocked Japan for only sending money during the war. Those commentators stopped laughing when Captain Taosa Ochiai and six Japanese naval vessels steamed eight thousand miles into the blazing summer heat of the Persian Gulf.

Why did Japan send four tiny wooden-hulled minesweepers, Hikoshima, Yurishima, Awashima, and Sakushima, instead of steel destroyers? Because Iraq had planted Italian-made Manta bottom mines on the seafloor that detonated the instant they sensed the magnetic field or engine hum of a steel hull.

Only non-magnetic hulls built of timber could float over them without blowing up.

Working in 120-degree heat alongside the U.S. Navy, Japanese minesweepers took on the most dangerous shallow sectors where sunken oil tankers and deadly Manta mines waited.

When sonar spotted a mine on the bottom that mechanical cables could not cut, Japanese explosive ordnance divers strapped on flippers, swam down into the murky water by hand, and placed explosive charges right next to live warheads.

Across ninety-nine straight days under the desert sun, Japan's wooden boats destroyed thirty-four deadly mines without losing a single sailor.

On their final day in the Gulf, U.S. Navy commanders stood at attention and saluted the sunburned Japanese crews who had cleared the sea in silence.

Real allies do not boast on television. They take the deadliest sector and clear the path for their friends.

This remains an unconfirmed assessment, not evidence that such an operation has been ordered or is imminent.

cvn-73.t: 🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Inside the carrier keeping the world's oil moving: US jets fly into Hormuz every night to shoot down Iranian missiles aimed at tankers What the Wall Stre…
cvn-73.tx:
🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Inside the carrier keeping the world's oil moving: US jets fly into Hormuz every night to shoot down Iranian missiles aimed at tankers

What the Wall Street Journal saw aboard the USS George Washington:

• F-35Cs and F/A-18s launch nightly with electronic-warfare jets, radar planes and sub-hunting helicopters to build an umbrella over tankers in a strait just 20 miles wide

• More than 3,000 commercial ships escorted through in six months, Gulf oil exports now above prewar levels, and CENTCOM marking 1.5 billion barrels shipped since summer

• The US says 95% of traffic passes safely and pilots report a 100% intercept rate when they're on station with missiles, though Iran sometimes fires at more ships than they can cover

• October was the most violent month for shipping since the war began, with more than 35 incidents logged by UKMTO

• 50,000 US troops and 20 Navy ships in the region, carriers setting modern records for days at sea without a port call, destroyer tours extended again

• The Navy's top admiral says sailors "need a port call" and is setting up a repair hub on Diego Garcia

• Washington's efforts to build an international coalition to share the job have gone nowhere

The mission is working, and that's the best argument against a strike: oil is flowing, Iran's economy is collapsing, so hold the line indefinitely.

The catch is the people doing the holding.

Every month adds $2 to $3 billion, more worn-out jets and longer stretches away from home for crews who were promised relief, and the White House now has to decide whether the next week brings a short, intense campaign or tells those sailors the blockade is their job for the foreseeable future.

Source: Wall Street Journal / Writer: Daniel

cvn-76.t: Laura Montero never thought her fun cruise to Mexico would end on a U.S. naval carrier surrounded by 3,000 sailors... The 14-year-old owes her life to the men…
cvn-76.tx:
Laura Montero never thought her fun cruise to Mexico would end on a U.S. naval carrier surrounded by 3,000 sailors...

The 14-year-old owes her life to the men and women of the USS Ronald Reagan, one of the largest aircraft carriers in the Navy, who saved her in a mission worthy of Hollywood script.

. . . 

In December 2007, 14-year-old Laura Montero from Albion, Illinois, was vacationing with her family on the Dawn Princess cruise ship off the coast of Baja California, Mexico, when she suddenly fell violently ill. Her appendix ruptured, presenting a life-threatening medical emergency while the ship was hundreds of miles out at sea and far from standard civilian surgical care.

With the cruise ship unable to reach land quickly enough, a distress call was answered by the nearby nuclear-powered U.S. Navy aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan, which was returning from a training tour. The massive warship altered its course and raced through the night. At around 5:00 a.m., a helicopter launched from the carrier to close the final 175-mile gap. Because there was no space to land on the cruise liner, a Navy medic was lowered onto the deck in a basket to retrieve Laura, placing her on an antibiotic drip before hoisting her into the aircraft.

Brought safely aboard the USS Ronald Reagan, Laura underwent a successful emergency appendectomy performed by the ship’s surgeon just hours later. Her mother was later flown out to reunite with her on the carrier, and Laura completed her journey back to mainland San Diego aboard the warship, fully recovering from the ordeal thanks to the extraordinary coordinated rescue.

Because the USS Ronald Reagan was a classified military warship, special diplomatic and naval clearance had to be swiftly coordinated to allow a civilian cruise passenger onto a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, marking an exceptionally rare instance of the U.S. Navy executing such a medical evacuation.

#drthehistories

al-dhafra.t: 🇮🇷⚔️🪖🇺🇸🇧🇭‼️The American Base Targeted 159 Times by Iran The Al Dhafra air base in the UAE, hosting a range of reconnaissance, communication, and support equipm…
al-dhafra.tx:
🇮🇷⚔️🪖🇺🇸🇧🇭‼️The American Base Targeted 159 Times by Iran

The Al Dhafra air base in the UAE, hosting a range of reconnaissance, communication, and support equipment, is a key node in the network of US and allied air operations in the Persian Gulf. This base was targeted 159 times during the Iran-Iraq War (Ramadan War).

The equipment stationed at this base connected reconnaissance, information transmission, command, and air operation support elements; a system that can be described as the "eyes, brain, and arm of air operations."

Information from the base's radars and reconnaissance aircraft was combined to create a common picture of the regional situation, which was then provided to the Al Udeid air operations center. Communication centers and satellite data reception facilities also served as a link for transmitting this information to commanders and operational units.

In the operational section, the 380th Air Expeditionary Wing managed missions related to reconnaissance aircraft, fighter jets, tankers, and air support. Large fuel storage tanks and aircraft maintenance facilities also provided the necessary support for the continuity of these missions.

The presence of US, UAE, and French forces gave Al Dhafra a multinational status, making it one of the key points for connecting the air power of these countries in the region.

The diversity of these targets indicates that in the attacks, in addition to aircraft, the necessary infrastructure for detection, reconnaissance, data transmission, command, and the continuation of operations was also a target. However, the targeting of each of these facilities, in itself, does not necessarily indicate the extent of the damage or its removal from the operational cycle.

The operational consequence highlighted in this account is the transformation of Al Dhafra from a support base into a point vulnerable to repeated attacks. This situation forces the US to allocate part of its capabilities and resources to protecting the base, dispersing equipment, and maintaining communication between the components of the network.

Farsna

prince-sultan.tx:
Saudi Arabia's Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman worked the phones with at least 6 defence chiefs in a single day, Pete Hegseth, France's Catherine Vautrin and Greece's Nikos Dendias among them. In the same window, according to reports, he sent Tehran a message through the Pakistan and Turkey channel: NO attacks will be launched from Saudi soil if Iran stops threatening the kingdom.

Riyadh is buying insurance from BOTH sides at once.

From the West it wants air defence and political cover while Houthi missiles and drones keep hitting its airports and oil sites. The strike on Riyadh's King Khalid airport on 10 October killed at least 12 people. From Iran it wants the Houthi tap turned down, and the price on offer is its own territory, kept out of any American campaign.

For Washington the territory pledge is the expensive part. Prince Sultan Air Base and Saudi airspace carry a lot of weight in any sustained US air war on Iran, and the kingdom has now told Tehran they are off limits. The smaller Gulf states hosting US forces just got a Saudi precedent to point to the next time they want to say no.

Tehran gets a split in the Gulf without firing a shot, and the Houthis show exactly what they are worth to Iran as a lever.

And Pakistan and Turkey, tied to Riyadh by the defence pact signed in August, are the ones carrying the messages, a seat at a table Washington used to run alone.

Iran's official line has been that it does not control the Houthis. If Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia fall off sharply in the next 2 to 3 weeks, that line will not survive the evidence.

Signal, Not noise!

diego-garcia.t: As negotiations fail, the Islamic Republic is threatening Europe with missile attacks. The Islamic Republic has released a harrowing video threatening Europe w…
diego-garcia.tx:
As negotiations fail, the Islamic Republic is threatening Europe with missile attacks.

The Islamic Republic has released a harrowing video threatening Europe with military retaliation and warning that European countries could face missile attacks.

The cinematic video was published by Iran in Arabic, an Arabic-language account that presents itself as the Islamic Republic’s voice in the Arab world, and framed as a “dangerous warning” from the regime’s armed forces.

Set across European streets, subway stations and cafés, it shows a regime figure appearing on public screens while crowds carry signs reading “NO MORE BLOOD,” “NO MORE AGGRESSION” and “NO MORE LIES.”

The message attempts to address Europeans directly while implying that their cities and civilians could face consequences if their governments continue supporting American and Israeli military action.

This was not an isolated propaganda release.

On the same day, Kayhan, which is closely connected to the Supreme Leader’s circle, warned that American and NATO facilities “in the heart of Europe” could be attacked. It named military sites in Cyprus, Greece, Romania, Albania, Italy and Britain.

Hamshahri simultaneously published a map marking military sites across nine European countries under the threatening headline “We’ll see what happens.”

Regime commanders have also declared that earlier geographic limits no longer apply. They now claim missile ranges of between 4,000 and 5,000 kilometres, placing much of Europe within their threatened strike zone.

The Islamic Republic has already moved beyond propaganda:

▪️ A drone struck RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus during the wider conflict.

▪️ The regime attempted long-range missile strikes against the joint American-British base at Diego Garcia.

▪️ Iranian missiles travelling westward were intercepted over Turkish territory.

▪️ European intelligence services have uncovered IRGC-linked assassination, arson, surveillance and sabotage operations across the continent.

▪️ British authorities charged two men over activity near RAF Fairford that the British government assessed was highly likely coordinated from Iran and almost certainly directed by the IRGC.

The pattern combines overt military threats with deniable covert action. Regime media publishes maps and videos. Commanders expand the declared target zone. IRGC networks use criminal proxies and operatives to test European security from within.

The timing is significant. Negotiations have failed to produce an agreement, the Islamic Republic has rejected the latest American response and military reinforcements are moving into the region.

The regime is now trying to frighten Europe away from supporting the next campaign by making European governments believe that their bases, infrastructure and populations could become targets.

This is not diplomacy from a government seeking coexistence. It is coercion from a regime responding to failed negotiations by expanding its threats from the Persian Gulf to Europe itself.

incirlik.t: A CREW DOG’S LIFE: Who can relate? 🙋‍♂️ 3AM on the flight line, and the world’s waiting like a caffeine-fueled adventure that doesn’t give a damn about your sl…
incirlik.tx:
A CREW DOG’S LIFE: Who can relate? 🙋‍♂️

3AM on the flight line, and the world’s waiting like a caffeine-fueled adventure that doesn’t give a damn about your sleep. You’re going somewhere else, carrying something different, and you’ll do it again tomorrow. Move the mission. 

There I am, coffee in one hand, flight bag in the other, eyes still half-glued shut, shuffling out to our big beautiful C-141 or C-17 beast under those harsh ramp lights. The “bag drag.”

The air’s crisp, the jet’s APU or power cart are already humming that low, throaty growl, as the jet wakes up for a global joyride. When it starts up, it barks at you. But that’s a good sign. And, the bittersweet smell of diesel exhaust and jet fumes. You grow to love it. I can’t explain it. It always felt like “home” no matter where in the world we were. 

Crew piles in: loadmasters cracking jokes, engineers double-checking the flyability of this metal marvel, and me sliding into the left seat thinking, “Alright, Lord, let’s do this again.”

It’s inherent. Not a lot of creative thought required. The crew, like a group of ants taking orders from the queen, automatically dives into their respective duties and checklists like clockwork. No direction needed here. It’s symbiosis. 

We crank the engines, taxi out into the dark, ramp lights fading into a world of blue and white lights, suck down some awful coffee, tell a few jokes, and blast off as the sun’s still thinking about showing up. 

The possibilities were endless. Could be one hop to Ramstein for fuel and some bratwurst, next leg to Incirlik where the pita bread’s fresh, the hookah’s are smoking, and the tension’s thicker than the Turkish coffee. Buy your pistachios here. 

Then it’s “wheels up” again. Maybe Diego Garcia for a quick dip in that insane blue water and warm beer, or over to Yokota where the ramen and beer hits different at 0200 local. And where I met my wife. 

Skipping across continents like stones on a pond, chasing daylight, dodging weather, and hauling everything from the SEALS, to the 82nd Airborne, to nuclear weapons, to Thanksgiving turkeys. Hell, once I flew a single generator to Nouadhibou, Mauritania. 

And a bunch of liquor to American embassies throughout the world. 

You land in one country for thirty minutes, grab a weird local snack that’ll haunt your stomach for days, chat with the ground crew in broken English and hand signals, sign some funky foreign forms pretending to know what they were, then you’re back in the air chasing the next sunrise. 

Jet lag? What jet lag. This is the life: stars above, stars on the flag on your sleeve, and the pure rush of knowing you’re part of the greatest airlift machine the world has ever seen. And we mattered, bigly. My country gave me a heavy jet and said “fly here.” It still blows my mind. 

No two days are ever the same. No two sunrises the same. 

Just pure, unfiltered freedom with a 🇺🇸 patch on your shoulder and a whole lot of “hold my coffee, I got this.”

God bless the @usairforce, @AirMobilityCmd, and the greatest group of Airmen history has ever seen. Best damn job I ever had.

akrotiri.t: UK expands military backing for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen despite rising civilian death toll —— According to an investigation by Declassified UK, Britain’s Min…
akrotiri.tx:
UK expands military backing for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen despite rising civilian death toll
——
According to an investigation by Declassified UK, Britain’s Ministry of Defense (MoD) has expanded its military assistance to Saudi Arabia, deploying Royal Air Force (RAF) Typhoon fighter jets and providing critical aerial refueling for Saudi airstrikes targeting Yemen.

The increased support was authorized by British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, who previously advocated for an arms embargo against Riyadh over its civilian casualty record in Yemen, but is now presiding over direct British involvement as Saudi strikes hit civilian centers.

Data from the Yemen Data Project reveals that Saudi airstrikes caused more civilian casualties last month than in any single period since 2022, resulting in at least 66 deaths and 90 injuries—including eight children.

Among the deadliest incidents was a September 22 strike on a residential home in Mokha that killed six civilians, followed days later by an attack on a market in the Al-Taiziyah district of Taiz that killed seven and injured 40 others.

Despite the rising toll, London agreed to send up to 20 Voyager aerial refueling sorties from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus with their transponders deactivated, while deploying Typhoons from Qatar to support Saudi air operations without charging the kingdom for the military assistance.

The escalation follows the collapse of a four-year UN-brokered ceasefire in July, triggered when Saudi-led forces bombed Sanaa International Airport. In response to the breakdown, Yemen's Armed Forces have launched retaliatory drone and missile strikes against strategic targets inside Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

While ten leading British trade unions and human rights monitors have demanded an immediate halt to UK military collaboration, British officials maintain that RAF deployments serve strictly "defensive counter air" purposes to protect regional allies.

whiteman.t: Ask any American infantryman why he never lets an A-10 Warthog pilot pay for his own beer, and he will tell you about a day like December 2, 2010. Sixteen sold…
whiteman.tx:
Ask any American infantryman why he never lets an A-10 Warthog pilot pay for his own beer, and he will tell you about a day like December 2, 2010.

Sixteen soldiers from the 201st Engineer Battalion of the Kentucky Army National Guard were clearing a mountain road out of Kandahar, Afghanistan, when rocket-propelled grenades crippled their first four vehicles at once.

Heavy machine-gun fire poured down from fortified stone positions along the ridgeline, pinning the sixteen Americans in a kill zone with nowhere to retreat.

After forty minutes of brutal combat, Specialist Mauricio Arias and Sergeant Joseph Parker looked at their rifles and realized the platoon was down to its final magazine of ammunition.

Rather than wait to be overrun and executed, the sixteen soldiers prepared to fix bayonets and charge straight up the hill on foot.

Then two A-10 Warthogs from the 303rd Fighter Squadron dropped out of the sky.

In the lead cockpit sat Captain Tony Roe, callsign Crack. On his wing flew Captain John Tice, callsign Sapper, a former enlisted U.S. Army combat engineer who knew exactly what it felt like to be bleeding in the mud below.

Calling the platoon leader on the FM radio, Roe asked the soldiers to pop a smoke grenade and declared Emergency Close Air Support.

Why is that declaration so rare?

Because declaring Emergency Close Air Support means the pilot personally accepts full legal responsibility if a single round strikes friendly troops.

On his first pass, Roe squeezed the trigger of his thirty-millimeter cannon, but a digital elevation glitch in the targeting computer sent the shells high over the ridge.

Without wasting ten seconds, Roe switched off the computer's elevation data, keyed in the altitude manually by hand, and dove back into the wall of machine-gun fire.

Flying low enough for the soldiers to read the numbers on his fuselage, Roe unleashed seven high-explosive rockets just forty meters from the American trench while Tice made six consecutive strafing passes with his thirty-millimeter Gatling gun.

To the sixteen men on the ground, that low tearing roar sounded like angels singing.

When the smoke cleared, thirty-two enemy fighters were dead, and every single American soldier walked out alive.

Nine years later, at Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri, Arias and Parker sat in the audience and stood with tears in their eyes to salute the two pilots as they received the Distinguished Flying Cross.

To a politician, the A-10 is an old budget line, but to an infantryman on his last magazine, that ugly gray jet is a brother coming down from heaven.

pearl-harbor.tx:
🇺🇸 Remember "BIG A" 

For some of the men aboard USS Arizona, surviving the explosion meant facing another nightmare: the ship was burning, and so was the water around her.

Commissioned in October 1916, USS Arizona (BB-39) was a Pennsylvania-class battleship armed with twelve 14-inch guns. She served through World War I without fighting a major naval engagement, then spent the interwar years on exercises, cruises, and fleet maneuvers.

By December 1941, she had been in service for a quarter of a century.

On the morning of December 7, "Big A" lay moored along Battleship Row at Pearl Harbor, with the repair ship USS Vestal alongside. Shortly before 8 AM Japanese aircraft swept over the harbor. Alarms sounded, and men raced to their battle stations.

Minutes later, an armor-piercing bomb penetrated Arizona’s forward decks. Her forward ammunition magazines exploded.

A towering fireball engulfed the forward part of the battleship. The blast tore through her structure, and she settled onto the harbor bottom. Fires continued burning for two days.

Arizona lost 1,177 sailors and Marines, nearly half of all Americans killed at Pearl Harbor.

For those who survived the initial destruction, escape could mean crossing burning decks or entering water covered with flaming oil. Wounded men struggled to move. Others tried to help shipmates whose bodies had been terribly burned.

Lieutenant Commander Samuel G. Fuqua, knocked unconscious early in the attack, recovered and helped direct firefighting and evacuation. His composure gave other men the courage to keep working amid the devastation. He would receive the Medal of Honor.

Above the bridge, six sailors were trapped by the flames. Among them were Donald Stratton and Lauren Bruner. Both had suffered severe burns. From Vestal, sailor Joe George spotted them and threw across a line. The men secured a heavier rope, then pulled themselves hand over hand toward the neighboring ship, suspended above the burning water.

Their burned hands had to carry their weight.

All six reached Vestal. Reaching safety, however, did not mean that all would live. Stratton later recalled that two died of their burns in the hospital that day. Stratton himself endured months of treatment. Eventually medically discharged, he recovered sufficiently to rejoin the Navy and fight in the Pacific.

USS Arizona would never return to sea.

Parts of her superstructure and armament were salvaged: Three of USS Arizona’s 14-inch guns fought again after Pearl Harbor. Salvaged from her No. 2 turret, refurbished, and installed aboard USS Nevada in late 1944, they bombarded Japanese positions on Iwo Jima and Okinawa in 1945. 

But the shattered hull remained where she had fallen. More than 900 of her dead were never recovered. The ship became their grave.

On May 30, 1962, the USS Arizona Memorial was dedicated above the wreck. Designed by architect Alfred Preis, its white structure spans the sunken battleship. Inside the shrine room, the names of the fallen are engraved in marble.

Even now, fuel oil still seeps from Arizona’s wreck, rising to the surface and spreading into rainbow-colored slicks. Often called "the black tears of the Arizona", these droplets are a visible reminder that the ship below still carries traces of that December morning.

Visitors can leave the memorial and return to shore. More than 900 of the men they have come to remember are still aboard. 🕯️🇺🇸

yokosuka.t: If you ask any U.S. Navy captain in the Seventh Fleet why America's most powerful warships never want to leave Yokosuka, Japan, they will not point to a treaty…
yokosuka.tx:
If you ask any U.S. Navy captain in the Seventh Fleet why America's most powerful warships never want to leave Yokosuka, Japan, they will not point to a treaty. They will point to two thousand Japanese master craftsmen in hard hats waiting inside a 150-year-old stone dry dock.

Keeping the U.S. Seventh Fleet ready to deter conflict across the Indo-Pacific requires constant, grueling hull and combat-system repairs.

Why does the United States Navy not simply sail its damaged or aging warships back to Pearl Harbor or San Diego for maintenance? Because steaming five thousand miles back across the Pacific pulls a frontline warship off patrol for months when every day counts.

Inside Fleet Activities Yokosuka sits Dry Dock Number 1, built out of hand-cut granite stone blocks by Japanese stonemasons in 1871. More than a century and a half later, those ancient stone walls still hold the weight of billion-dollar American Aegis destroyers without cracking an inch.

Working inside those six dry docks is the U.S. Naval Ship Repair Facility and Japan Regional Maintenance Center, powered by over two thousand Japanese master welders, pipefitters, shipwrights, and electrical engineers.

Many of these Japanese artisans are second- and third-generation craftsmen whose fathers and grandfathers repaired American warships in the exact same docks.

When the U.S. Seventh Fleet flagship USS Blue Ridge, the oldest operational warship in the U.S. Navy, or an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer comes in from rough seas, Japanese shipwrights and American sailors climb under the massive steel hull shoulder to shoulder.

Through freezing winter nights and sweltering summers, Japanese welders lay down flawless steel seams that U.S. Navy inspectors call the gold standard of the Pacific.

Warships are made of steel. Alliances are kept afloat by the men with welding torches in the bottom of the dock.

yokosuka.t: September 12, 2001. Armed US sailors lock down the main gate of Yokosuka Naval Base and brace for another attack. Within hours, a crowd of Japanese citizens be…
yokosuka.tx:
September 12, 2001. Armed US sailors lock down the main gate of Yokosuka Naval Base and brace for another attack.

Within hours, a crowd of Japanese citizens begins walking toward the concrete barriers.

The commander of the base was a 48 year old US Navy Captain. His name was Robert Francois.

Hours earlier, on the night of September 11 in Japan, four hijacked planes had struck New York, the Pentagon, and Pennsylvania. Half a world away, the 20,000 Americans stationed at Yokosuka, home of the US Seventh Fleet, were cut off from home. Phone lines to the United States were jammed. Young sailors stood watch in full combat gear behind steel barricades, terrified for their families and expecting further strikes.

They felt completely alone.

Then the sun came up over Tokyo Bay.

One by one, residents from the city of Yokosuka walked up to the armed guards at the main gate. An elderly woman bowed in silence and placed a bouquet of white chrysanthemums on the pavement.

Not a word.

Then came schoolchildren carrying strings of 1,000 folded paper cranes.

By afternoon, the security barrier was buried under a wall of fresh flowers, candles, American flags, and handwritten notes. On scraps of paper, Japanese neighbors had written in careful English: "We cry with you" and "America, stay strong."

Here's where it gets even more moving. Ten days later, on September 21, when the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk departed Yokosuka, thousands of Japanese citizens and Maritime Self Defense Force sailors lined the harbor waving American flags to see the crew off.

Captain Robert Francois retired from the Navy in 2003 after 30 years of service. Ten years after 9/11, when the March 2011 tsunami devastated northern Japan, the Seventh Fleet sailed straight from Yokosuka to launch Operation Tomodachi, rescuing thousands of Japanese families.

On the darkest morning in modern American history, a city that once fought the US Navy made sure its sailors never cried alone.

yokosuka.t: Last Friday, I took my fifty eight year old boss, Director Sato, to an American sports bar in Yokosuka. I ordered a basket of traditional Buffalo Wings and two…
yokosuka.tx:
Last Friday, I took my fifty eight year old boss, Director Sato, to an American sports bar in Yokosuka.

I ordered a basket of traditional Buffalo Wings and two draft beers.

When the plate arrived, Director Sato put on his reading glasses and leaned over the table. He stared at the small, orange pieces of meat for a long time.

"Wait," Director Sato said quietly.

"Yes, sir?" I asked.

"A buffalo is a giant American cow that weighs two thousand pounds," he said. "Why are its wings the size of my thumb?"

I nearly choked on my beer.

"Sir," I said. "Buffaloes cannot fly. These are chicken wings."

Director Sato frowned deeply. "Then why did the menu say Buffalo Wings?"

"They were invented in a city called Buffalo, in New York," I explained.

He processed this information in complete silence.

Inside I said: HIS BRAIN IS REWRITING AMERICAN GEOGRAPHY.

"I see," he said, nodding slowly. "In Japan, we have Kobe beef. In America, they have Buffalo chicken. It is a regional title of honor."

He picked up a wing, dipped it into the white cup of blue cheese dressing, and took a bite.

His eyes lit up. Then the cayenne pepper hit his throat. He coughed once, grabbed a raw celery stick like a lifeline, and chewed it furiously.

"The spicy sauce attacks you," he gasped, "and the green vegetable saves your life. This is a brilliantly balanced ecosystem."

I want to be accurate here: he ate twelve wings by himself, sweating through his suit jacket.

At 8:30 PM, he raised his hand toward the American bartender and shouted with complete confidence:

"Excuse me! One more plate of the flying cow, please!"

yokosuka.t: My wife's aunt is a midwife. Last month, after 34 years, she retired. Her hospital is near the U.S. Navy base in Yokosuka. In 34 years, she delivered 412 Ameri…
yokosuka.tx:
My wife's aunt is a midwife. Last month, after 34 years, she retired.

Her hospital is near the U.S. Navy base in Yokosuka. In 34 years, she delivered 412 American babies.

At her retirement party, she gave a speech. Half of it was about American fathers.

"When I started," she said, "Japanese fathers waited in the hallway. Or at the office.

American fathers came into the room. They only ever leave for one reason."

Some of what she said:

"They pack a bag for themselves. Snacks. Chargers. A speaker. One had a playlist called BABY DAY. The baby did not care for it."

"They coach. 'Breathe, babe. You got this. Big push.' Like it's fourth and goal. The mothers tell them to be quiet. They get quieter. They never stop."

"They cry. The bigger the man, the louder. A Navy chief with a neck as wide as my waist cried so hard, I almost gave HIM the oxygen."

"I write the weight in grams. 3,290. The father does math on his phone, runs into the hallway, and announces it like a final score. 'SEVEN POUNDS, FOUR OUNCES!' Strangers clap. Thirty-four years, I still don't know what an ounce is."

"Every one of them introduces himself. 'Hey, buddy. I'm your dad.' As if the baby might ask for ID."

"They inspect the car seat for 40 minutes. Then they drive home at the speed of a bicycle with the hazard lights on."

Then she stopped smiling.

"And sometime in the first hour, every single one of them walks out to the hallway alone and calls his father.

Big men. Quiet men. Men who told me they hadn't spoken to their fathers in years.

They all call."

"In 2019, a young sailor called. It went to voicemail. He left a long message. 'Dad. It's a boy. He's got your ears. We named him after you.'

The next day, he called again. And the next.

On the fourth day, his wife told me. His father had died eight months before. His mother never cancelled the phone. She still pays for it, so she can hear his voice.

He called that number every day until they took the baby home."

She looked at the room for a long time.

"In 34 years, I learned one thing about American men.

The moment they become fathers, they become sons again."

When she sat down, nobody clapped for a while.

Then, one by one, the Japanese men in the room stood up and walked out to the hallway.

I was the third.

yokosuka.t: I have an urgent Halloween question for Americans. Tonight, my wife and I walked past an American neighbor's house in Yokosuka. No one was home, but there was…
yokosuka.tx:
I have an urgent Halloween question for Americans.

Tonight, my wife and I walked past an American neighbor's house in Yokosuka.

No one was home, but there was a giant plastic bowl full of candy sitting on a chair outside the front door.

Taped to the bowl was a handwritten sign that said: "Happy Halloween! Please take one."

My wife stopped walking. She stared at the unattended bowl in pure disbelief.

In Japan, we have unmanned vegetable stands in the countryside where people leave coins in a box. We understand the honor system for adults buying radishes.

"Wait," my wife whispered. "They left five pounds of chocolate in front of unsupervised children in the dark?"

She looked around the street as if looking for hidden cameras.

"Is this a trap?" she asked me. "Is the homeowner hiding in the bushes to test the moral character of the neighborhood kids?"

Please tell me the truth. Does the second kid who walks up to that bowl actually take just one piece? Or does that bowl become completely empty in four minutes?

September 9, 1942. A Japanese floatplane launches off the coast of Oregon to drop firebombs on the US mainland. Fifty five years later, that exact Oregon town…
yokosuka.tx:
September 9, 1942. A Japanese floatplane launches off the coast of Oregon to drop firebombs on the US mainland.

Fifty five years later, that exact Oregon town named him an honorary citizen.

His name was Nobuo Fujita.

At 30 years old, Warrant Officer Fujita became the only pilot in history to bomb the continental United States during wartime. Flying a tiny Yokosuka E14Y floatplane launched from the submarine I 25, he dropped two incendiary bombs over Wheeler Ridge near Brookings, Oregon. Rain soaked forests kept the flames small, and nobody was hurt.

Twenty years later, in 1962, the Junior Chamber of Commerce in Brookings came up with an unthinkable idea. They invited the man who bombed them to be the guest of honor at their Azalea Festival.

Fujita was terrified it was a trap.

Before boarding his flight to America, he packed his family's 400 year old samurai sword in his luggage. He promised himself that if the townspeople pelted him with rotten eggs or put him on trial as a war criminal, he would use the blade to take his own life in the traditional way.

It wasn't a trap.

Three thousand Americans lined the streets of Brookings to shake his hand and welcome him. Stunned by their grace, Fujita walked into the town hall and handed over his 400 year old family sword as a gift of peace.

Here's where it gets even deeper. Fujita never stopped paying the town back.

In 1985, he brought three students from Brookings to Japan at his own expense after his company went bankrupt. In the 1990s, when he heard Brookings was struggling to build a new public library, the elderly pilot mailed checks totaling 15,000 dollars from his modest savings.

In September 1997, Nobuo Fujita died of lung cancer in Japan at age 85. Days before he passed, Brookings made him an honorary citizen.

The following year, his daughter Yoriko flew to Oregon and buried a portion of his ashes at the exact bomb site in the forest, right beside a redwood seedling he had planted himself.

He flew to Oregon twice: once to burn their forest down, and once to plant a tree where his ashes now rest.

yokosuka.t: In Ginza, ordering sushi that is not on the menu gets you a polite refusal. In my neighborhood in Yokosuka, a giant young marine from Texas walked into our tin…
yokosuka.tx:
In Ginza, ordering sushi that is not on the menu gets you a polite refusal.

In my neighborhood in Yokosuka, a giant young marine from Texas walked into our tiny eight seat sushi bar, nervous and sweating.

He wanted to order a Tekka Maki, the classic tuna roll.

Instead, he pointed at the glass case and asked the 68 year old master for a "Texas Roll."

Master Watanabe did not blink. He did not correct him.

He sliced a piece of bluefin tuna twice as thick as usual, added pickled jalapeno from his own lunch, and shaped it with two sharp claps of his hands.

"One Texas Roll," the master said, placing it on the cedar board.

That marine came back every Friday for two years until his deployment ended.

When a new batch of sailors walked in last night and asked what the house special was, Master Watanabe pointed to a wooden plaque on the wall.

It is the most expensive item on the menu now.

kadena.t: 🇯🇵 - A Japanese bomber landed on its belly at an American airfield. Then armed men climbed out. Their mission had only just begun. On the night of May 24–25, 1…
kadena.tx:
🇯🇵 - A Japanese bomber landed on its belly at an American airfield. Then armed men climbed out. Their mission had only just begun.

On the night of May 24–25, 1945, Japanese aircraft approached Okinawa, where American forces had captured airfields and put them to work against their former owners.

Among the attackers were Mitsubishi Ki-21 "Sally" bombers carrying an unusual cargo: commandos equipped with demolition charges, grenades, and small arms.

These were men of the Giretsu airborne raiding force.

Their targets were the American aircraft parked at Yontan and Kadena. Destroying them on the ground could weaken the fighter cover that was intercepting Japan’s kamikaze attacks.

There was no extraction plan. They were expected to land, destroy as much as possible, and fight on.

The operation began to unravel before most of the raiders reached their objectives. Aircraft turned back, failed to find their targets, or were shot down.

But one bomber got through.

It made a wheels-up landing at Yontan. Commandos emerged onto the American airfield.

Although drawn from airborne troops, they had not parachuted in. Their aircraft had delivered them directly into the target.

They attacked parked planes and fuel installations with grenades and incendiary charges. Aircraft burned. Fuel dumps containing roughly 70,000 gallons of gasoline went up in flames.

For hours, defenders hunted the raiders through the darkness. Confusion compounded the damage: the Marine Corps’ official account records Americans accidentally firing on their own men.

By the time the last attacker was killed, several American aircraft had been destroyed and many others damaged.

The raid had inflicted real damage, but it could not reverse the battle for Okinawa.

These men are sometimes called “kamikaze paratroopers.”

Share this overlooked chapter of the Pacific War, and follow @Vanguard_WW2 for more stories behind the familiar history.

kadena.t: On July 22, 2012, a United States Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon pilot out of Misawa Air Base had to eject into the freezing North Pacific Ocean 250 miles nort…
kadena.tx:
On July 22, 2012, a United States Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon pilot out of Misawa Air Base had to eject into the freezing North Pacific Ocean 250 miles northeast of Hokkaido, Japan.

For the next six hours, the American pilot, callsign JEST 73, floated alone in a tiny one-man life raft, using his own flight helmet by hand to bail icy water out so he would not sink.

Above the clouds, three U.S. Air Force KC-135 Stratotankers from Kadena and McConnell refused to leave him, circling in shifts while relaying his coordinates to Japanese and American rescue controllers.

One hundred miles away, Captain Mike Gruninger and Second Mate Jim Dowling aboard the American container ship MV Manukai ordered maximum engine RPMs and turned their giant ship around.

At the exact same moment, a Japanese fishing boat named the Hokko Maru raced through the swells toward the same spot.

Because the 700-foot American container ship was too tall to pluck a man safely from a rubber raft in rolling waves, the Japanese fishermen on the Hokko Maru pulled the shivering American pilot from the sea and brought him right alongside the Manukai's lowered gangway ladder.

All twenty-one American sailors lined the rails cheering as he climbed aboard, where the ship's satellite phone was already dialed to his wife and two little girls.

In the Pacific, an American wingman does not just fly an F-16. Sometimes he steers a Japanese fishing boat.

kadena.t: If someone asks you how much two newborn babies are worth to the United States Air Force, tell them the exact price: two 200-million-dollar C-17 Globemaster II…
kadena.tx:
If someone asks you how much two newborn babies are worth to the United States Air Force, tell them the exact price: two 200-million-dollar C-17 Globemaster III warplanes and an airborne refueling tanker over the Pacific Ocean.

In May 2009, two tiny babies at the U.S. Naval Hospital in Okinawa, Japan were fighting for every breath. One was twenty days old. The other was a nine-month-old infant in severe heart and lung failure.

To survive the seven-thousand-mile flight to Texas for open-heart surgery, the nine-month-old needed an external heart-lung bypass machine called ECMO.

Within hours, Lieutenant Colonel Dr. Daniel Dirnberger, Major Dr. Melissa Tyree, and the 59th Medical Wing turned a massive C-17 cargo jet at Kadena Air Base into a flying neonatal intensive care unit.

Then the first C-17 suffered a mechanical failure right before takeoff while the babies' portable incubators began running low on medical air and battery power.

The Air Force did not blink. Crews rushed the babies into the Kadena clinic for oxygen and immediately pulled a second 200-million-dollar C-17 Globemaster III onto the runway.

And because landing in Alaska for fuel would cost five precious hours, the 168th Air Refueling Wing scrambled a tanker from Eielson Air Force Base to refuel the C-17 in mid-air over the Pacific, delivering both babies safely to Texas in fourteen hours flat.

A superpower is not measured by the tanks in its cargo bay. It is measured by how fast it clears that bay for two tiny cribs.

kadena.t: 🇺🇸 His guns froze... So he brought down a Japanese aircraft with his Corsair’s propeller. Then he flew home! May 10, 1945. Above Okinawa, four Marine Corsairs…
kadena.tx:
🇺🇸 His guns froze... So he brought down a Japanese aircraft with his Corsair’s propeller. Then he flew home!

May 10, 1945. Above Okinawa, four Marine Corsairs climbed after a Japanese reconnaissance aircraft.

Two couldn’t climb any farther. Captain Kenneth Reusser and his wingman, First Lieutenant Robert R. Klingman of VMF-312, kept going.

They even fired off ammunition to lighten their aircraft.

At roughly 38,000 feet, Reusser got within range. He hit the Japanese aircraft, then exhausted his remaining ammunition.

Klingman moved in to finish the attack.

He pressed the trigger.

Nothing.

According to the Marine Corps’ official history, the cold had frozen his guns. The enemy aircraft was still flying, and its rear gunner was still a threat.

Klingman closed in until his Corsair’s spinning propeller struck the Japanese aircraft’s tail.

One attack wasn’t enough. He came back.

Accounts describe three passes before he had cut away enough of the tail surfaces to send the aircraft plunging toward the sea.

That’s a whole different level of badass. But this tough guy still had to get home!

His Corsair had taken bullets. Its propeller and engine cowling were battered. Pieces of the Japanese aircraft were lodged in his own.

Yet he reached Kadena and landed without injury.

A photograph taken afterward shows him examining the damaged propeller—the part that had kept his fighter airborne and become his weapon.

Klingman received the Navy Cross. His citation explicitly credits him with destroying the enemy aircraft by severing its tail surfaces with his propeller.

The damage was photographed. The action was recorded. And the pilot lived to tell the story.

For more WWII stories, follow @Vanguard_WW2 

📷 USMC: Robert R. Klingman inspecting his damaged Corsair propeller at Kadena, May 10, 1945.

camp-humphreys.t: A war in Korea would be settled in part on factory floors in Alabama and Arkansas. North Korea would open with two kinds of fire at once, artillery aimed at Se…
camp-humphreys.tx:
A war in Korea would be settled in part on factory floors in Alabama and Arkansas.

North Korea would open with two kinds of fire at once, artillery aimed at Seoul and missiles aimed at American bases such as Osan and Camp Humphreys. Each needs its own answer, because shells cannot stop a missile in flight and Patriot and THAAD interceptors are not built to stop shells.

South Korea stocks first for the opening 30 days of a war, so what follows would depend on how fast two separate industrial bases can produce. Lockheed Martin delivered 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, about a dozen a week for the US military and allied Patriot users.

In 2026 both bases began to grow. Lockheed broke ground on a new plant in Troy, Alabama, and won a THAAD contract worth up to $35 billion that aims to quadruple output to 400 a year, while Hanwha, a South Korean company, announced a $2.2 billion campus at Pine Bluff Arsenal in Arkansas to make 155mm propellant charges.

That places a South Korean company inside the American supply chain that would back South Korea in a war, so the alliance would draw on shared factories as well as shared bases. Both projects run on seven-year timelines, and a credible factory floor may weigh more in Pyongyang's calculations than a full shelf.

This is Part 3 of Rate of Fire, a five-part series on how munitions production would shape a major war in each theater, and Part 4 turns to the Pacific.

All three men in this photo at Arlington, JFK, Grant Stockdale, and James Forrestal, died suddenly and unexpectedly. One was shot in Dallas. The other two fell from high windows.

Forrestal, the first Secretary of Defense, strongly opposed U.S. recognition of Israel in 1948. He warned it would damage American interests in the Middle East and create long-term problems. In 1949 he was found dead after falling from a 16th-floor window at Bethesda Naval Hospital. Official ruling: suicide. His brother Henry insisted it was murder. He told author Cornell Simpson that James “positively did not kill himself,” that he “was the last person in the world who would have committed suicide,” and that he believed someone had strangled him and thrown him out the window. Forrestal himself had complained he was being followed by “Jews or Zionist agents” and Communists.

JFK later ran into friction with Israel over its nuclear program at Dimona. His administration pressed for inspections and also pushed efforts to force the pro-Israel lobby to register as a foreign agent under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. He was assassinated in 1963.

Stockdale, standing with JFK at Forrestal’s grave in this 1963 photo, was a close Kennedy friend and former ambassador. Days after the assassination he met with Bobby and Ted Kennedy, then told friends the “world was closing in.” The day before he died he told his lawyer, in rambling fashion, that “those guys” were trying to get him and spoke about the assassination. The next day he fell from the 13th floor of a Miami office building. Official ruling: suicide.

Three men. Three sudden deaths. One photo.

qt.t:
Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one. “Bibi calls Trump about it every day,” says an informed observer.

Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.

To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated set

dimona.tx:
Tucker Carlson reports that Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Donald Trump to launch a nuclear strike on Iran. Before that idea gains any ground in Washington, its consequences need to be understood. More than 180 countries renounced nuclear weapons under a set of explicit promises. A nuclear attack on Iran would show those promises to be worthless.

The bargain is written into the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty itself. Under Article II, non-nuclear-weapon states agreed not to acquire nuclear arms. In return, they were promised three things: the inalienable right to peaceful nuclear energy, good-faith negotiations toward disarmament by the nuclear powers, and - when the treaty was extended indefinitely - assurances that nuclear weapons would not be used against them, noted by the Security Council in Resolution 984. In Iran’s case, the first promise has already been broken: its peaceful programme has been sanctioned and bombed. The second has gone unmet for decades. A nuclear strike would break the third.

The regime urging this strike has never accepted any part of that bargain. Israel refuses to join the NPT, has never acknowledged the arsenal it built at Dimona, and has ignored Security Council Resolution 487 calling on it to place its nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards. When Mordechai Vanunu exposed the programme, Israeli agents abducted him in Rome and he spent 18 years in prison. Under the Begin Doctrine, Israel claims the right to bomb any state in the region it suspects of seeking the capability it already possesses, while demanding total transparency from its neighbours and accepting none for itself. At the same time, Israel stands accused of genocide and of widespread war crimes and crimes against humanity. Its forces have repeatedly violated the sovereignty of neighbouring states through cross-border strikes and occupations, and it has pursued an openly aggressive posture across the region. Its prime minister is wanted by the International Criminal Court. This is the war criminal now urging Washington to use the most destructive weapon ever built against a member of the treaty his regime has spent half a century evading.

Iran’s record points the other way. It negotiated the JCPOA, which the Security Council endorsed unanimously in Resolution 2231, and the IAEA confirmed its compliance in report after report. Washington walked away anyway. When Iran returned to the table, it was attacked twice: days before a scheduled round with U.S. envoys, and hours after talks in Geneva that Oman’s foreign minister said had brought the two sides close to a genuine agreement.

Article X allows any party to withdraw if extraordinary events related to the treaty have jeopardised its supreme interests. A nuclear attack on a member that negotiated, complied, and kept returning to diplomacy would hand that argument to every other member. Islamic countries will rightly see an ethno-supremacist and racist ideology behind this use of nuclear weapons. A nuclear strike against a Muslim-majority nation, urged by a regime that has long defined itself in ethno-religious terms and that has never accepted the restraints of the NPT, would be read not as a narrow security measure but as the expression of a deeper hierarchy of peoples. That perception would further erode confidence in the treaty among its Islamic members and accelerate momentum toward withdrawal. The treaty rests on a single premise: that a state can give up the bomb and still be safe. If that premise fails in Iran, parliaments, politicians, and publics across the membership will start asking whether staying in serves their security. Some governments will decide that it does not. Withdrawals, individual or collective, would follow, and the non-proliferation regime would simply not survive them.

@TuckerCarlson

fordow.t: Trump is reportedly contemplating using nuclear weapons against Iran's facilities. This is exactly and precisely where all those who advocated withdrawing from…
fordow.tx:
Trump is reportedly contemplating using nuclear weapons against Iran's facilities. This is exactly and precisely where all those who advocated withdrawing from the JCPOA, and then "maximum pressure," wanted him to be.

Trace the timeline. First, they claimed the JCPOA was a bad deal that needed fixing. Remember the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' motto, "fix it or nix it"? Then they lured him out of the agreement by insisting it could not be fixed. Then they lobbied for the most extreme economic measures imaginable under maximum pressure. Then the narrative quietly shifted: economic pressure alone would not work, they said, and diplomacy with Iran required a "credible threat of military force." Just short of calling for war.

Once the use of force was normalized, they set about getting him to actually use it. Report after report argued that designating Iran's official armed forces, the IRGC, as a terrorist organization, and then assassinating Iran's top general, would make Tehran cave. It didn't. But the ice had been broken. From then on, every step was an escalation, and every diplomatic initiative that might have eased tensions or produced a peaceful settlement was attacked and buried.

Then came the strike on Fordow, alongside Israel. Then the war in February, in which they got him to cross every red line and pushed a settlement further out of reach than ever.

Running in parallel all these years was a campaign to persuade Washington that diplomacy with Iran is a waste of time and that the only option worth keeping on the table is the military one. Iran is just "buying time," they said. Iran never honors its commitments, they said, even as IAEA inspectors verified its compliance over and over. You can't negotiate with the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism. Iran cannot be trusted. Iran is weak. Why bother negotiate with a “significantly weakened Iran” when you can simply use force to extract concessions?

So much for "weak"!

Every one of these assumptions has proved false. Yet instead of asking why they were wrong at every turn, they read each failure as proof that the last measure was too mild. 

And so here we are. Openly discussing war crimes, threatening to wipe out power plants and bridges, bombing civilian infrastructure and even weighing nuclear weapons have all become ordinary instruments of policy. 

They took a president who brandished "The Art of the Deal" and sold himself as the ultimate dealmaker, and turned him into a man deciding whether to become the first leader since Truman to use a nuclear weapon. Against whom? A country that was already at the negotiating table, prepared to reach an equitable agreement.

So don't let them ever claim this was about a bad nuclear deal that needed correcting. It was always about Israel's destructive agenda, carried into Washington by its lobbies, its mouthpieces and its PR firms.

There is an old fable about a frog dropped into a pot of water that is heated so slowly it never thinks to jump. Each degree feels bearable, because it is only one degree warmer than the last. The frog never notices the moment the water starts to boil. Washington is that frog. And the water is already boiling.

Before the strikes, experts assessed that Iran could potentially move from 60% to weapons-grade material in days to weeks if it retained sufficient enrichment capacity. WHERE IS THE URANIUM?

How much survived?
Where is it stored?
And has Iran retained or rebuilt the capability needed to enrich it further?

More than 70 weeks after Operation Midnight Hammer, those are questions the world still needs answered.

fordow.t: 🇮🇷|Araghchi to Merz: "There Will Be No More Red Lines." Germany's Welcome of the Airstrikes Has Been Noted. And So Has Its Bill. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghch…
fordow.tx:
🇮🇷|Araghchi to Merz: "There Will Be No More Red Lines." Germany's Welcome of the Airstrikes Has Been Noted. And So Has Its Bill.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X on Saturday, 31 October 2026: "When U.S. and Zionist airstrikes against Iran began last year, Mr. Merz welcomed these attacks, describing them as the execution of 'Europe's dirty work.'"

Then the line that matters: "A sum of 100 billion euros cannot be compared to the decisive and devastating response that the Iranian armed forces will deliver to anyone who dares to violate our nation's sovereignty; there will be no more 'red lines.'"

The Foreign Minister named the co-belligerent.

Friedrich Merz is not an observer. He is the German Chancellor. When US and Israeli aircraft bombed Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan in June 2025, Merz did not call for restraint. He welcomed the strikes. He called them Europe's dirty work, a phrasing that admits the continent wanted the bombing done and preferred that someone else's pilots do it. Araghchi has now put that admission on the record from the Iranian foreign ministry's own account.

That is not a diplomatic exchange. That is a charge sheet.

Read what "no more red lines" means.

For two decades Iran operated inside a restraint doctrine. It stayed in the NPT. It accepted IAEA inspections. It negotiated the JCPOA. It absorbed the US withdrawal from that deal in 2018. It absorbed the assassination of its scientists. It absorbed the bombing of its safeguarded facilities and the IAEA's silence about who dropped the bombs. Every stage of that restraint was a red line Iran chose not to cross.

Araghchi has just announced the end of that doctrine. "No more red lines" is not a threat aimed at one country. It is the formal abandonment of the restraint architecture. It tells Berlin, Washington, and Tel Aviv that the calculation that kept Iran inside limits no longer applies.

The 100 billion euros is the German rearmament bill, and Araghchi sized it against the wrong column.

The 100 billion euro figure is the German defence fund Berlin created to rebuild the Bundeswehr. Araghchi compared it to the response the Iranian armed forces will deliver. His point is arithmetic, not rhetoric: money buys hardware, and hardware does not answer what Iran answers with. German defence procurement is a budget line. Iranian retaliation is a doctrine that has already been demonstrated against Saudi airports at Najran, Khamis Mushait, and Abha.

The deeper layer Berlin does not want examined.

Germany presents itself as a diplomatic actor in the Iran file. It was an E3 member of the JCPOA negotiations. It signed the deal. Then it stood with Washington after Washington destroyed the deal. Then it welcomed the bombing campaign that hit the facilities the deal had verified.

Berlin supplied the political cover. The United States and Israel supplied the aircraft. Merz called it Europe's dirty work because he understood the division of labour. Germany wanted the Iranian nuclear programme bombed without German aircraft in the sky and without German crews in the cockpits. It got what it wanted and then told its public it was a spectator.

Araghchi has refused the spectator framing. He has put Merz in the co-belligerent column, by name, from the foreign ministry's official account.

The contradiction Washington and Berlin cannot resolve.

Germany is not an NPT nuclear weapons state. It shelters under NATO's nuclear umbrella. It hosts US nuclear weapons at Büchel. It lectures Iran about NPT compliance while sitting inside a nuclear sharing arrangement. It welcomed the bombing of safeguarded facilities inside a non-nuclear-weapons state that was, at the moment of the bombing, under IAEA inspection.

The IAEA withdrew its inspectors from Iran in June 2025 because of the safety risk of the strikes. The Security Council has since drafted resolutions blaming Iran for the resulting loss of continuity. Germany voted for the architecture that produced that outcome

qt.t:
Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one. “Bibi calls Trump about it every day,” says an informed observer.

Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.

To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated set

fordow.tx:
This is hysterical nonsense. 
Trump and Netanyahu will not nuke Pickaxe Mountain. 

Trump has indicated on numerous occasions he despises nuclear weapons and would prefer “denuclearization.” Israel does not want to be the country that breaks the norm against nuclear weapons use and triggers a race for nukes in its region. 

What may be on the table is disabling Tehran’s access to Pickaxe’s tunnel entrances—which the United States did rather effectively using 30 Tomahawk missiles against the Esfahan nuclear complex—in 2025. The Esfahan tunnels house highly enriched uranium and a new enrichment plant. The regime has not restored access all this time, and blocking access has allowed for monitoring to detect such activity.

Pickaxe has the potential to serve as a new enrichment and weaponization facility, more deeply buried that Fordow. Iran reportedly moved surviving centrifuges there in the fall of 2025. It hasn’t been constructing the facility in recent weeks, having fortified the tunnels against a possible strike. 

Let’s remember: Tehran could resolve all of this tomorrow by simply letting the IAEA go there or agreeing to verifiably dismantle it—something Iran has refused for years. It has also been continuing work on other undeclared sites struck during 2025 and 2026. 

It would not be surprising if the U.S. and Israel act against Pickaxe to prevent the Iranians from restoring a nuclear weapons pathway—indeed, it would be irresponsible to leave such a decision to their successors. 

But it won’t be a nuclear strike.

This announcement comes after public discussions in the media about a possible attack by the United States on a fortified underground Iranian nuclear complex near Mount Pikes (near Natanz).

Among the recommendations:

* Do not look at the flash.
* Lie on the ground behind the nearest sturdy shelter, covering your head and face with your hands.
* Wait out two shockwaves – the direct and the reflected – do not get up until they have passed.
* Seek shelter from radiation in a shelter and stay there for at least 24 hours.

natanz.tx:
After reading @TuckerCarlson’s post below, felt like searching on Google: What are the dangers of nuking a country such as Iran? Below was google’s response: 

A nuclear attack—whether an actual detonation of a nuclear weapon or a catastrophic strike on a nuclear facility (such as the Bushehr reactor or enrichment sites like Natanz and Fordo in a country like Iran)—carries catastrophic, multi-layered dangers: 

1. Immediate Physical and Health Destruction
•Vaporization, Blast, and Thermal Waves: An actual nuclear detonation causes instant vaporization near ground zero, massive blast waves that shatter buildings, and intense thermal heat triggering giant firestorms. 
•Mass Casualties & Collapse of Healthcare: Tens of millions or millions of people would face immediate death or severe burns, trauma, and radiation sickness. Remaining medical infrastructure, hospitals, and pharmacies would be rapidly overwhelmed or destroyed. 

2. Radiological Release and Environmental Contamination
•Attacks on Nuclear Reactors or Enrichment Sites: Hitting a nuclear power plant (like Bushehr) or spent fuel ponds can breach containment, releasing dangerous radioactive isotopes—such as Iodine-131, Cesium-137, and Polonium-210—into the air and water. 
•Regional Water and Desalination Crises: In a region like the Persian Gulf, radioactive contamination of seawater threatens vital desalination plants in neighboring countries (such as Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia), potentially cutting off drinking water supplies within days. 
•Fallout and Air Currents: Radioactive clouds can cross national borders, matching or recalling historical cross-border contamination events like Chernobyl. 

3. Long-Term Health and Genetic Consequences
•Radiation Illness & Cancers: Survivors experience acute radiation syndrome (hair loss, internal bleeding, immune system collapse) followed decades later by high rates of radiation-induced cancers (such as thyroid cancer) and increased risks of birth abnormalities or leukemia in future generations. 
•Food & Famine Risks: Widespread soil and water contamination, combined with the collapse of local agriculture and distribution networks, risk mass starvation and severe malnutrition. 

4. Global and Regional Geopolitical Fallout
•Regional Escalation and Arms Races: A strike on or by a nation like Iran risks immediate retaliatory spirals, drawing in regional and global powers, destabilizing the Middle East, and unraveling international non-proliferation treaties. 
•Global Climate Disruption: Large-scale nuclear exchanges or massive fires inject millions of tons of soot into the upper atmosphere, potentially causing global cooling ("nuclear winter") and global agricultural failure.

pickaxe.t: The use of a nuclear weapon in Iran may not destroy the mountain, but it destroys an entire model of international relations. As has been floated in recent day…
pickaxe.tx:
The use of a nuclear weapon in Iran may not destroy the mountain, but it destroys an entire model of international relations.

As has been floated in recent days, Netanyahu has been working toward an operation with tactical nuclear missiles against Iran. 

This would be different from using a bomb like the ones we saw in Japan, which were designed as strategic weapons to destroy entire cities.

Tactical warheads have a lower destructive yield, usually between 1 and 50 kilotons. 

They are designed to eliminate specific military targets on the battlefield, bases, ports, or armored columns, without triggering an instantaneous global apocalypse. 

Most of these tactical missiles are, in theory, meant to detonate in the air, hundreds of meters above their targets, avoiding ground contact and leaving radiation that dissipates within weeks in the affected area.

The problem is that the plan reported by Tucker Carlson would involve detonating the Pickaxe mountain, as Donald Trump also once promised. That would be a radioactive catastrophe of a different order from an airburst hundreds of meters above a region, something that already strikes me as absurd enough.

All of this is terrifying, but the use of a tactical nuclear weapon would mean changing the paradigms on which international relations are built. 

The use of tactical missiles and direct attacks against a regional power like Iran would redefine traditional concepts of state sovereignty, respect for borders, and, above all, the logic of global nuclear deterrence.

In international law and relations between states, territorial sovereignty is the fundamental pillar. A direct attack with tactical missiles would transform that dynamic and bring an end to traditional red lines. 

It would demonstrate that possessing a robust conventional army or a vast territory no longer prevents invasion or direct bombardment by technologically superior forces. 

This would consolidate the idea that states can violate the sovereignty of others on the basis of anticipated threats, a precedent we already live with, but one that would reach another level with nuclear weapons.

The most dangerous shift would occur in how countries view nuclear weapons. Historically, deterrence works on the premise that the cost of attacking a country is too high. 

If Iran, a country on the threshold of nuclear development, is attacked in a conventional and tactical manner, the geopolitical message would first and foremost be one of encouragement to proliferate.

This scenario would turn the global board into a far more unpredictable environment, where fear and the rush to acquire weapons of mass destruction would replace diplomacy and economic containment.

pickaxe.t: NEW ANALYSIS: Tucker Carlson's nuclear strike warning seems to be drawing all the headlines right now, and in many ways, rightfully so. But it's missing the po…
pickaxe.tx:
NEW ANALYSIS: Tucker Carlson's nuclear strike warning seems to be drawing all the headlines right now, and in many ways, rightfully so.

But it's missing the point in my opinion.

Undoubtedly, a nuclear strike against Pickaxe Mountain would open up Pandora's Box on the use of nuclear weapons, with no shortage of countries that would be itching to use them. As a result, this should certainly be condemned.

However, in my own assessment, I think that the LIKELIHOOD that President Trump uses nuclear weapons against Iran is fairly low. Possible? Certainly. Likely? No.

But there IS something that is highly likely, and while not as truly existential to humanity, would come with enormous consequences... And that is the maintenance of the current status quo in the Iran War, or any continuation of the war whatsoever at this point.

In anything short of a return to the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding, or a removal of American forces and the blockade from the region, there WILL be global economic devastation that would rival the Great Depression. This isn't "unlikely", this is HIGHLY likely, and I think that it is something that is being sidelined right now as a result of this nuclear warning.

There is no credible argument that Iran can escalate across the Gulf at will. Look at how easily Ansar Allah (Houthis) are penetrating Saudi airspace and blasting energy infrastructure and airports, including the Aramco Headquarters in Dhahran. Simultaneously, Iran is striking moving vessels, under US air cover, with multiple Marines on board in the Strait of Hormuz... And your argument is Iran CAN'T devastate the Gulf if forced to?

As of now, there are effectively four options in the Iran War for President Trump to pursue. Three are catastrophic, and one is not.

1) First use nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain - Catastrophic

2) Comprehensive bombing campaign on economic and civilian infrastructure in Iran that would warrant immediate and devastating Iranian retaliation - Catastrophic

3) A continuation of the current status quo, which if you believe would eventually risk the collapse of Iranian society, Iran will respond and we can't defend - Catastrophic

4) Make the necessary concessions to Iran that President Trump AGREED to under the MOU at Versailles, or lift the blockade and remove our troops from the region and reset the negotiations under non-aggressive circumstances for Iran that do warrant retaliation - NOT CATASTROPHIC

Whether it be the first use of nuclear weapons, whether it be a comprehensive bombing campaign, or whether it merely be a continuation of the current status quo, there is ZERO scenario in which there is not enormous and catastrophic consequences imposed on all of humanity.

Except an end to war.

Tucker Carlson's nuclear warning should be taken very seriously, but don't miss the forest for the trees here:

All of this is catastrophic unless President Trump deescalates this conflict.

parchin.t: An Islamic Republic official admits the regime lied about the massive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes, blaming explosions at military sites on nat…
parchin.tx:
An Islamic Republic official admits the regime lied about the massive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes, blaming explosions at military sites on natural events such as thunder and lightning.

Mohammad Sadegh Koushki, a hardline regime figure appearing on state television, described the deception openly. Israeli strikes on the Kermanshah drone base were publicly blamed on thunder and lightning, while repeated attacks on missile facilities and other sensitive military sites were never announced.

This was not an isolated cover story. It was part of a systematic campaign to hide the scale of the regime’s military losses while exaggerating its remaining strength and supposed victories.

“Gas leaks” are another standard cover story used when explosions occur at or near sensitive military, missile and IRGC-linked facilities. Like the lightning excuse, the explanation allows the regime to disguise a possible attack or act of sabotage as an ordinary domestic accident.

In June 2020, a massive nighttime explosion near the Parchin military complex was officially blamed on a gas leak at a storage facility in a public area. Satellite imagery later revealed extensive damage and scorch marks at the adjacent Khojir missile-production complex, directing attention toward a facility associated with missile propellants rather than the harmless location described by the regime.

The same pattern resurfaced after the July 2025 explosion at the Pamchal 9 complex, a residential building connected to the Armed Forces Judicial Organization. State and judiciary media blamed owner negligence and a gas leak. Residents reportedly disputed the explanation, saying the building was not connected to the municipal gas network and that the damage across several floors did not resemble an ordinary domestic explosion.

Other explosions near military and industrial facilities have been attributed to gas leaks, aging infrastructure or routine accidents. In some cases, regime-linked outlets initially raised the possibility of Israeli involvement before deleting those references and adopting the official accident narrative.

When U.S. and Israeli strikes damaged drone bases, missile-production facilities, air defences, naval assets and command centres, the regime responded with silence, weather excuses and restrictions on reporting from the affected areas. Evidence of destruction was concealed from Iranians because acknowledging it would expose the failure of the military system that consumed enormous national resources while proving unable to protect itself.

The regime simultaneously manufactured stories of overwhelming retaliation. State television and IRGC-linked outlets claimed Iranian missiles had destroyed strategic Israeli sites, devastated American forces and achieved extraordinary success rates. Many of these claims relied on recycled footage, manipulated imagery, fabricated casualty figures or targets that independent evidence showed remained operational.

The strategy was simple. Hide Iranian losses, invent enemy losses and preserve the illusion that the regime remained in control.

The actual damage was substantial, although American assessments differed over its permanence. U.S. Central Command described severe degradation across Iran’s missile, drone, naval and defence-industrial infrastructure. It reported that launch rates had fallen dramatically and that large portions of production capacity and major naval assets had been destroyed.

More cautious American intelligence assessments concluded that Iran retained significant missile stocks, mobile launchers and access to many underground facilities. That means the regime was badly damaged but not disarmed. It still possesses dangerous capabilities and could rebuild parts of its arsenal over time.

Both assessments, however, contradict the Islamic Republic’s claim that its forces emerged largely intact or even stronger.

Koushki’s admission reveals why official Iranian accounts cannot be trus
